characterList.name: Dr. Cherry Ng

content_metadata.description: Dr. Cherry Ng shares her expertise in radio astronomy, the search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI), and her involvement in the Square Kilometer Array (SKA) Observatory.

qAndA.question: What is the equivalent of the CNRS in Spain, according to Dr. Ng?

qAndA.answer: To study nearby galaxies, monitor the galactic plane, and analyze data from the nearest billion stars in search of technosignatures.
qAndA.question: What is the primary goal of the Breakthrough Listen program?

qAndA.answer: Because radio emissions are relatively cheap to produce, travel through the Earth's atmosphere, and can be detected from ground-based telescopes.
qAndA.question: Why is the radio spectrum the primary focus for SETI research?

qAndA.answer: Narrowband drifting signals, which are distinct from broader radio frequency interference generated by human technology.
qAndA.question: What type of signal are SETI researchers primarily looking for?

qAndA.answer: That investing in SETI research is crucial, even if the chances of immediate success are uncertain. Discovering extraterrestrial intelligence would be a profound scientific breakthrough with implications for humanity's understanding of itself and its future.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: I work at the CNRS in France, which stands for the Centre National de la Recheche
de la Chessillaan-Tifique, which is like Fasique in Spain. I work at the Institute located in
Allion, which is a small town, about one hour south of Paris. My main scientific interest is in
the search for radio transients, such as pulsars, fast radio bursts, but also in the detection of
city, which aims to look for signals from extraterrestrial civilizations. My job is 100% research,
which means I don't have obligations to teach or do any other things, so I can really set my own
agenda of how I spend my research time. Although I do enjoy very much working with students, so I
supervise the number of student projects. I also contribute to different aspects of the academic
life, for example, serving as the co-chair of the SK Science Working Group, where I hope to help
define the future direction of radio astronomy. Since I started my scientific career about 14
years ago as a student, I already heard about the Square Kilometer, the SKA project, and I have
been looking forward to working with this, what will be the most sensitive radio telescope ever
constructed. I think the SKA is really cool because it's the best science instrument that we will
have, but also the fact that it is so international, it's a project of multi-countries that we really
bring the world together to build something that will advance our knowledge of the universe.
So when the SKA contacted me to be the co-chair of the Crado of Life Science Working Group in 2022,
I did not hesitate and agree to it immediately. In 2023, I was also invited to join the Science and
Engineering Advisory Committee for the SKA, where we meet about three times a year, and we hear
about the progress of the SKA, and we provide our expert recommendation on the progress.
The Crado of Life Science Working Group of the SKA really cares about the search of the origin of
lives, and this is a really broad topic. It includes things like planet formation, for example, the Earth,
how it was formed, and how life emerged from it, or things like physics and chemistry of young stars,
as well as the search for extraterrestrial intelligence elsewhere in the universe.
And so the Science Working Group of Crado of Life, I see it as a platform to facilitate all these
kinds of collaborations. About ten years ago, there was the preparation for the SKA white book,
so there was the magnetic activity for the Science Working Group at that time. It was a little bit quiet
now, but SKA is really starting to build. A lot of progress is being made, so I think once again,
the Science Working Group is playing a major role, being a place for the scientists to get
ourselves ready for the day when the SKA will become available in the very near future.
One of my research interests is in SETI, and what is that about? SETI is the search for
extraterrestrial intelligence. We look for techno signatures, which are advanced signals from technology
of extraterrestrial intelligence life. It is analogous to the study of biosignature. Where scientists
look for molecular lines like water that might show a sign of life. SETI, as a community, has really
grown a lot in the last years, a lot thanks to support from private donors. One main example is
the breakthrough listen foundation. It is a 10-year, $100 million dollar program in the search for
extraterrestrial intelligence. The main goal of breakthrough listen is to study 100 nearby galaxies,
monitor the galactic plane and also to analyze data from the nearest billion stars.
Very few lessons have really provided a lot of opportunity to fund young people to join the
field and to contribute to the research, as well as to support observing program on many of the
most sensitive radio telescopes around the world, including parks in Australia, green bank in the
USA, the very large array, as well as meacad in South Africa.
The way we search for techno signatures, the majority of work has been done in the radio spectrum,
and why is that? It's because radio emission is relatively cheap to produce. Just look at ourselves
as human technology. We have been using radio telecommunications for decades now, so we might expect
any extraterrestrial civilizations to do the same. Radio emission is also one of the few windows
that we can go through the atmosphere, which means we can easily detect it from Earth without having
to send space satellite detector that costs more money. Then in radio spectrum, what are we looking
for? We think that the most likely signals that we will detect are narrow-banned drifting
human telecommunications technologies. We have been using filters to concentrate information
in a small range of the electromagnetic spectrum. So this is the idea of searching for narrow-banned
signal. It is also very distinguishable from astrophysical signals, which tend to be much more
broadband in nature. So what we're talking about, it's like hurts with signal really, really narrow
compared to astrophysical ones. Then we expect these signals to be drifting in time and frequency,
because imagine that there is this telecommunication from an exoplanet that we detect from Earth,
and the exoplanet will have a differential acceleration with respect to the motion of our Earth.
So we will see the signal drifting in time and frequency. If you talk to any radio astronomer,
they will be dreading of this thing called RFI, which is radio frequency interference. These
are signals generated by human technologies such as spoons or televisions or satellites
that astronomers are unfortunately picking up in their observational data that is contaminating
the stars, the galaxy that they want to observe, which is so much weaker. We, when we search
for steady signal, basically we are trying to detect RFI from space, the RFI generated by the
extraterrestrial intelligence. I think the first kind of signal signature that we will detect,
like I explained earlier, will be these narrow-banned drifting signals. But more importantly,
I think it must be a signal that repeats. We cannot just see at once and say that this is
a steady signal because as Karm Sagan said some many years ago, extraordinary claims require
extraordinary evidence. So we need to be able to see the same signal multiple times in the same
location in the sky to be really sure that this is really nothing else, that it is real,
steady information. I think we will need to coordinate with as many radio telescopes as possible.
Everybody looking at this location, if we can all see it, then it helps to have more confidence
that the signal is true. Detecting techno signature, I think will be one of the most
important scientific discoveries of all time. I think it will completely change our perspective
as human. I think for a long time it seems like we are the only living things in the universe,
and even on Earth, we human have seen ourselves as the most advanced life form of all. If we detect
extraterrestrial intelligence, then they would more likely, or most likely, be more advanced than
us. So what does that mean? And I think studying the fate of the extraterrestrial intelligence will
really teach us a lot about our past, and importantly, our future, what leads in front of us.
Some people say it's a waste of money to look for extraterrestrial intelligence. Now, I remember
some years ago in the astronomy department, we had a very interesting discussion at the coffee time
where we were wondering, imagine if we can time travel to say 10,000 years later, and we can
get the answer of one astronomy question, what would it be? And a lot of people ended up deciding that
the only thing, the one thing that they want to know is their life outside, and have we made contact.
So I think our way alone is really one of the most profound questions we have. It captures the
imagination of not only scientists, but also the general public. Now, for people who say it's the
waste of money, I think what they are implying is that they don't think we'll detect any
signal any time soon. And perhaps I don't disagree. In fact, we have only search for a
setty signal in a very, very small fraction of the sky. So it is possible that there is
something out there, but we just haven't had the resources to really look properly. And I think
maybe with our current technology, we have not yet the sensitivity to detect these signals from
another planet that may be, may or may not be directing to the Earth, but if we don't start looking,
we'll never find.

youtube_description:
En marzo vino al IAA a dar un coloquio Severo Ochoa la Doctora Cherry Ng, la presidenta del grupo de ciencia de SKAO sobre "cuna de la vida" (Cradle of life) y una reconocida experta en temas de búsqueda de inteligencias extraterrestres (SETI).

Aprovechamos su visita para entrevistarla sobre este tema, que tanto apasiona a la ciudadania. ¿Hablamos de marcianitos verdes? Pues va a ser que no, eso hay que dejárselo a la ciencia ficción, pero sí nos explicó el concepto de "tecnomarcador", que nos ha parecido fascinante...

¿Quieres saber más? Para eso vas a tener que verte la entrevista, ¡merece la pena!


Edición: Celia Navas
